L32: # Enumeration of idempotents in planar diagram monoids
L33: ###### Abstract
L34: We classify and enumerate the idempotents in several planar diagram monoids: namely, the Motzkin, Jones (a.k.a. Temperley-Lieb) and Kauffman monoids. The classification is in terms of certain vertex- and edge-coloured graphs associated to Motzkin diagrams. The enumeration is necessarily algorithmic in nature, and is based on parameters associated to cycle components of these graphs.
L35: We compare our algorithms to existing algorithms for enumerating idempotents in arbitrary (regular $*$-) semigroups, and give several tables of calculated values.
L36: Keywords: Diagram monoids, partition monoids, Motzkin monoids, Jones monoids, Temperley-Lieb monoids, Kauffman monoids, idempotents, enumeration.

L43: ## 1 Introduction
L44: Diagram monoids arise in numerous branches of mathematics and science, including representation theory, statistical mechanics and knot theory [cite22†18 , cite23†5 , cite24†23 , cite25†28 , cite26†39 , cite27†22 , cite28†24 , cite29†26 ]. Many studies of diagram monoids have been combinatorial in nature [cite30†15 , cite31†10 , cite32†14 , cite33†9 , cite34†8 , cite35†27 , cite36†12 ], and idempotents have played a large role in several of these works.
L45: Historically, it is interesting to note that products of idempotents [cite35†27 , cite36†12 , cite37†13 ] were understood several years before the idempotents themselves were [cite33†9 ]; this is largely due to the fact that diagram monoids have natural anti-involutions that give them regular $*$-semigroup structures [cite37†13 , cite38†34 ], meaning that arbitrary idempotents are products of simpler idempotents known as projections (see Section cite7†2 for definitions).
L46: In [cite33†9 ], classifications and enumerations were given for the idempotents in the partition, Brauer and partial Brauer monoids, and also for the idempotent basis elements in the corresponding diagram algebras. The current paper continues in this direction, focusing this time on planar diagram monoids, such as the Motzkin, Jones (a.k.a. Temperley-Lieb) and Kauffman monoids.
L47: However, the methods employed here are necessarily different to those of [cite33†9 ], as the planarity constraint means that the set symmetries used to study the monoids in [cite33†9 ] are no longer available. In fact, we believe that enumeration of the planar idempotents is inimical to closed-form solution; for one thing, the highly complex meandric numbers [cite39†7 , cite40†6 ] occur during the enumeration of Kauffman idempotents, as noted below in Section cite17†5 .
L48: We seek to fill this gap by presenting methods for computing the numbers of idempotents in the Motzkin, Jones and Kauffman monoids, with attention given to efficiency of the algorithms involved.
L49: The article is organised as follows. In Section cite7†2 , we describe two existing algorithms for enumerating the idempotents of arbitrary finite (regular $*$-) semigroups, commenting on their respective complexities in general and in the context of the Jones and Motzkin monoids in particular. Section cite8†3 develops a theory of idempotents in the Motzkin, Jones and Kauffman monoids. A key role is played by certain graphs, called interface graphs, associated to arbitrary Motzkin elements.
L50: These graphs are used to classify the idempotents in Proposition cite41†3.4 and Corollaries cite42†3.5 and cite43†3.6 , and then to enumerate them in Theorems cite44†3.16 , cite45†3.17 and cite46†3.19 ; see also Proposition cite47†3.15 . Section cite12†4 presents a number of algorithms, based on the theory developed in Section cite8†3 , that calculate the number of idempotents in the Jones, Kauffman and Motzkin monoids; C++ implementations of these algorithms can be found at [cite48†30 ].
L51: Finally, Section cite17†5 gives several tables of calculated values, including comparative run-times of the various algorithms.
L52: The reader is referred to the monographs of Higgins [cite49†19 ] and Howie [cite50†20 ] for background on semigroups in general, and to the introduction of [cite33†9 ] and references therein—in particular to foundational articles of Jones [cite24†23 ], Martin [cite25†28 ] and Halverson and Ram [cite22†18 ]—for background and relevant detail on the partition, Brauer and partial Brauer monoids.
L53: ## 2 Existing algorithms
L54: 
L55: In this section, we describe two existing approaches to counting idempotents in semigroups such as those we study in this article. The first applies to any finite semigroup, while the second applies to any finite regular $*$-semigroup; see below for the definitions. In Section cite17†5 , we will discuss the performance of these two approaches when applied to the diagram monoids we are concerned with, and we will compare them with the new algorithms presented in Section cite12†4 .
L56: The first approach to counting idempotents in an arbitrary finite semigroup $S$ is simple: create the elements of $S$, and then check if $x^{2}=x$ for each $x\in S$; see Algorithm cite51†1 . If the semigroup $S$ is generated by $A\subseteq S$, then $S$ can be enumerated using the Froidure-Pin Algorithm [cite52†16 ].
L57: If the complexity of multiplying elements in $S$ is assumed to be constant, then the complexity of the Froidure-Pin Algorithm is $O\big(|S||A|\big)$, so Algorithm cite51†1 has complexity $O\big(|S||A|+|S|\big)=O\big(|S||A|\big)$.

L70: The approach just described requires the creation of each element of $S$ in order to check which elements are idempotents. When $S$ is very large, this can be impractical, in terms of both space and time. The second approach improves on the first in the case that $S$ is a regular $*$-semigroup. To describe it, we must first recall some background.
L71: Recall from [cite38†34 ] that a semigroup $S$ is a regular $*$-semigroup if there is a unary operation ${}^{*}:S\to S$ such that $x^{**}=x$, $(xy)^{*}=y^{*}x^{*}$ and $xx^{*}x=x$ for all $x,y\in S$. For the remainder of this section, we fix a finite regular $*$-semigroup $S$. Recall that Green’s relations $\mathrel{\mathscr{R}}$, $\mathrel{\mathscr{L}}$, $\mathrel{\mathscr{J}}$, $\mathrel{\mathscr{H}}$ and $\mathrel{\mathscr{D}}$ are defined on $S$ as follows. Let $x,y\in S$.
L72: We say that $x\mathrel{\mathscr{R}}y$ if $xS=yS$, that $x\mathrel{\mathscr{L}}y$ if $Sx=Sy$, and that $x\mathrel{\mathscr{J}}y$ if $SxS=SyS$.
L73: The relation $\mathrel{\mathscr{H}}$ is defined to be the intersection of $\mathrel{\mathscr{R}}$ and $\mathrel{\mathscr{L}}$, while $\mathrel{\mathscr{D}}$ is defined to be the join of $\mathrel{\mathscr{R}}$ and $\mathrel{\mathscr{L}}$; that is, $\mathrel{\mathscr{D}}$ is the least equivalence on $S$ containing both $\mathrel{\mathscr{R}}$ and $\mathrel{\mathscr{L}}$.
L74: It is well known that ${\mathrel{\mathscr{D}}}={\mathrel{\mathscr{R}}}\circ{\mathrel{\mathscr{L}}}={\mathrel{\mathscr{L}}}\circ{\mathrel{\mathscr{R}}}$, and that ${\mathrel{\mathscr{D}}}={\mathrel{\mathscr{J}}}$ since $S$ is finite; see [cite50†20 , Chapter 2] for more background on Green’s relations. We write $E(S)=\{{x\in S}:{x^{2}=x}\}$ for the set of all idempotents of $S$. An element $x\in S$ is called a projection if $x^{2}=x=x^{*}$.
L75: The set of all projections of $S$ is denoted by $\operatorname{Proj}(S)$. The next result is true of any regular $*$-semigroup, whether finite or infinite; proofs of the various parts may be found in [cite53†21 , cite38†34 , cite54†35 ].

For any subset $A\subseteq S$, we will write $E(A)=A\cap E(S)$ and $\operatorname{Proj}(A)=A\cap\operatorname{Proj}(S)$ for the set of all idempotents and projections belonging to $A$, respectively. L114: Since $S$ is finite, it follows that $S$ has the stability property: namely, for any $x,y\in S$, $xy\mathrel{\mathscr{D}}x$ implies $xy\mathrel{\mathscr{R}}x$, and $xy\mathrel{\mathscr{D}}y$ implies $xy\mathrel{\mathscr{L}}y$; see [cite57†36 , Section A.2]. The various parts of the next lemma may be known, but we give proofs for completeness.
L115: ###### Lemma 2.3.
L116: 
L117: Let $S$ be a finite regular $*$-semigroup. Then
L118:

L120:

L125: for any $\mathrel{\mathscr{D}}$-class $D$ of $S$, and for any projections $x,y\in\operatorname{Proj}(D)$, $R_{x}\cap L_{y}$ contains an idempotent if and only if $xy\mathrel{\mathscr{D}}x$, in which case this idempotent is $xy$,

L131: ###### Proof.
L132: (i). Let $x\in\operatorname{Proj}(S)$. If $y\in[x]$, then $x=y\cdot a=a^{*}ya$ and $y=x\cdot b=b^{*}xb$ for some $a,b\in S$, so that $x\mathrel{\mathscr{J}}y$, whence $x\mathrel{\mathscr{D}}y$ as $S$ is finite. Conversely, suppose $y\in\operatorname{Proj}(S)$ and $x\mathrel{\mathscr{D}}y$. Then $x\mathrel{\mathscr{R}}a$ and $a\mathrel{\mathscr{L}}y$ for some $a\in S$. By Lemma cite55†2.1 (vi) and (vii), and since $x,y\in\operatorname{Proj}(S)$, we obtain $aa^{*}=xx^{*}=x$ and $a^{*}a=y^{*}y=y$.
L133: It follows that $y=a^{*}a=a^{*}aa^{*}a=a^{*}xa=x\cdot a$, and similarly $x=y\cdot a^{*}$, so that $y\in[x]$.
L134: (ii). Suppose first that $R_{x}\cap L_{y}$ contains some idempotent $e$. Since $e\mathrel{\mathscr{R}}x$, Lemma cite55†2.1 (vi) gives $ee^{*}=xx^{*}=x$, and similarly $e^{*}e=y$. Then $e=ee^{*}e=e(ee)^{*}e=(ee^{*})(e^{*}e)=xy$. Also, $xy=e\mathrel{\mathscr{R}}x$ implies $xy\mathrel{\mathscr{D}}x$.
L135: Conversely, suppose $xy\mathrel{\mathscr{D}}x$. Then stability gives $xy\mathrel{\mathscr{R}}x$. Since $xy\mathrel{\mathscr{D}}x\mathrel{\mathscr{D}}y$, stability also gives $xy\mathrel{\mathscr{L}}y$. Thus, $xy\in R_{x}\cap L_{y}$. Lemma cite55†2.1 (ii) gives $xy\in E(S)$.
L136: (iii). First note that the number of idempotents in $D$ is equal to the number of $\mathrel{\mathscr{H}}$-classes in $D$ containing an idempotent, since each $\mathrel{\mathscr{H}}$-class contains at most one idempotent. If $a\in D$, then $H_{a}=R_{a}\cap L_{a}$, and by Lemma cite55†2.1 (iii) and (iv) we have $R_{a}=R_{x}$ and $L_{a}=L_{y}$ for unique projections $x,y\in\operatorname{Proj}(D)$.
L137: That is, every $\mathrel{\mathscr{H}}$-class in $D$ is equal to $R_{x}\cap L_{y}$ for unique projections $x,y\in\operatorname{Proj}(D)$. By part (ii), just proved, this $\mathrel{\mathscr{H}}$-class contains an idempotent if and only if $xy\mathrel{\mathscr{D}}x$. ∎
L138: Parts (i) and (iii) of Lemma cite58†2.3 form the basis of the second approach to computing the number of idempotents in the finite regular $*$-semigroup $S$, given by a generating set $A\subseteq S$; see Algorithm cite59†2 . Roughly speaking, the steps of this algorithm are:

L151: Step (1) can be achieved using the action from (cite56†2.2 ) in a simple orbit algorithm whose input is the generators $A$; see [cite60†11 , Algorithm 1]. If the complexity of determining $x\cdot a$ is assumed to be constant, then the complexity of [cite60†11 , Algorithm 1], and hence the complexity of Step (1), is $O\big(|{\operatorname{Proj}(S)}||A|\big)$.
L152: By Lemma cite58†2.3 (i), the sets $\operatorname{Proj}(D)$ correspond to the strongly connected components of the action of $S$ on $\operatorname{Proj}(S)$ given in (cite56†2.2 ). These can be found using standard algorithms from graph theory, such as Tarjan’s [cite61†38 ] or Gabow’s [cite62†17 ], for example; see also the monograph of Sedgewick [cite63†37 ].
L153: The complexity of these algorithms, and thus the complexity of Step (2), is $O\big(|{\operatorname{Proj}(S)}|+|A|\big)$, which is bounded above by $O\big(|{\operatorname{Proj}(S)}||A|\big)$, the complexity of Step (1).
L154: If the $\mathrel{\mathscr{D}}$-classes of $S$ are $D_{1},\ldots,D_{r}$, and if these $\mathrel{\mathscr{D}}$-classes have $m_{1},\ldots,m_{r}$ projections, respectively, then Step (3) involves $m_{1}^{2}+\cdots+m_{r}^{2}$ products and checks for $\mathrel{\mathscr{D}}$-relatedness (modulo some optimisations discussed below). Thus, the total complexity of Algorithm cite59†2 is

L157: The $\mathrel{\mathscr{H}}$-classes in a single $\mathrel{\mathscr{D}}$-class of a semigroup all have the same size [cite50†20 , Lemma 2.2.3]. If the $\mathrel{\mathscr{H}}$-classes in the $\mathrel{\mathscr{D}}$-class $D_{i}$ have size $h_{i}$, then $|D_{i}|=m_{i}^{2}h_{i}$, since $D_{i}$ has $m_{i}$ $\mathrel{\mathscr{R}}$- and $\mathrel{\mathscr{L}}$-classes (Lemma cite55†2.1 (iii) and (iv)), and so

L160: This upper bound is realised if and only if $h_{i}=1$ for all $i$: i.e., if $S$ is $\mathrel{\mathscr{H}}$-trivial. In this worst case, the total complexity of Algorithm cite59†2 is $O\big(|{\operatorname{Proj}(S)}||A|+|S|\big)$. When we compare this to the complexity of Algorithm cite51†1 , which we noted above was $O\big(|S||A|\big)$, we see that Algorithm cite59†2 has a significant advantage if $|{\operatorname{Proj}(S)}|$ is small relative to $|S|$. Note that $|{\operatorname{Proj}(S)}|=m_{1}+\cdots+m_{r}$.
L161: We note that Algorithm cite59†2 , presented below, contains a number of simple optimisations. First, the $\mathrel{\mathscr{H}}$-class $H_{x}=R_{x}\cap L_{x}$ of a projection $x\in\operatorname{Proj}(D)$ always contains an idempotent: namely, $x$ itself (see Line cite64†6 ). L162: We also note that when $S$ is any of the diagram monoids we consider, the $\mathrel{\mathscr{D}}$-relation is given by equality of the ranks of elements of $S$, and is easily checked computationally; see Section cite8†3 for the definition of rank, and also [cite67†40 , cite68†25 , cite31†10 ] for more on Green’s relations on diagram monoids. Finally, we note that Algorithm cite59†2 can be derived from [cite60†11 , Algorithm 10], which counts idempotents in a fixed $\mathrel{\mathscr{R}}$-class.

L186: This paper mostly concerns the case in which $S$ is a Jones, Motzkin or Kauffman monoid. As noted above, the definitions of these monoids are given in Section cite8†3 , but here we make some brief comments relevant to the current discussion. For each non-negative integer $n$, we have a regular $*$-monoid $\mathcal{J}_{n}$ (Jones) and $\mathcal{M}_{n}$ (Motzkin). The sizes of these monoids, and the sizes of their sets of projections, are given (see [cite31†10 , cite69†3 , cite32†14 ]) by
L187:  | $$|\mathcal{J}_{n}|=C_{n},\hskip 10.00002pt|\mathcal{M}_{n}|=\mu(2n,0),\hskip 10.00002pt|{\operatorname{Proj}}(\mathcal{J}_{n})|=\sum_{r=0}^{n}\frac{r+1}{n+1}\binom{n+1}{\frac{n-r}{2}},\hskip 10.00002pt|{\operatorname{Proj}}(\mathcal{M}_{n})|=\sum_{r=0}^{n}\mu(n,r).$$  |
L188: Here, $C_{n}=\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}$ is the $n$th Catalan number; we interpret a binomial coefficient $\binom{m}{k}$ to be $0$ if $k$ is not an integer between $0$ and $m$; and the Motzkin triangle numbers $\mu(n,r)$ are defined by the recurrence
L189: 
L190:  | $\displaystyle\mu(0,0)=1,\hskip 10.00002pt\mu(n,r)=0$  |       if $n<r$ or $r<0$,  |
L191:  | $\displaystyle\mu(n,r)=\mu(n-1,r-1)+\mu(n-1,r)+\mu(n-1,r+1)$  |       if $0\leq r\leq n$ and $n\geq 1$.  |  | (2.4)
L192: The numbers $\mu(n,r)$ are also given by the formula
L193: 
L194:  | $$\mu(n,r)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}\binom{n}{j}\left[\binom{n-j}{r+j}-\binom{n-j}{r+j+2}\right].$$  |  | (2.5)
